for_you_if: you want a quick narrative experience
not_for_you_if: you expect branching paths to change the ending

cohorts.label: <2h refund window
cohorts.summary: Reviewers note the short runtime and retro instant messaging aesthetics, alongside repetitive typing mechanics and linear branching paths.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game takes about an hour or less to finish.

citations.review_text:
A short play, took me less than an hour to get to the end. The choices you make matter a lot and influence the different endings you could get. Starts off really sweet, turns bittersweet to just bitter :((. 
I really love the layout and all the sound effects in this game :D
If you have time, you should play it!

I played this on my Lenovo ThinkPad T480 (8th Gen Intel Core i5-8350U, 32GB RAM) running Linux Mint LMDE 7, and it ran flawlessly. No compatibility issues whatsoever.

Emily is Away is a love letter to the early 2000s internet era.

The branching narrative gives you some agency, but the story ultimately follows a fairly linear path. You'll make dialogue choices that affect the tone of conversations, but don't expect radically different endings on your first playthrough.

My biggest complaint? It's just too short. I finished the story in about an hour, and while that hour was enjoyable, I couldn't shake the feeling that this was more of a demo than a complete game. This makes perfect sense once you realize the developer's other games (Emily is Away Too and Emily is Away <3) continue and expand upon this universe. Think of this as the opening chapter of a larger story.

If you're looking for a quick, free dose of 2000s nostalgia with good writing and a relatable story, give it a try. Just go in knowing it's a brief experience that serves as a foundation.

Worth your time? Absolutely, especially since it's free. Just manage your expectations regarding length.

This game is incredibly simple, but somehow it hits harder emotionally than many big story games.

Emily is Away takes place entirely through an old-school chat program that looks like early 2000s AIM / Windows XP messenger. You create a username, pick a profile icon, and talk to Emily over several years of your life. It sounds basic, but the way the conversations unfold makes it feel strangely real.

What makes the game special is how relatable the story is. It captures that awkward teenage phase where friendships and relationships slowly drift apart. The typing system is also clever — you actually type responses, watch your character erase messages, and rewrite them like a real conversation.

The nostalgia factor is huge. The buddy icons, away messages, old computer sounds, and chat style perfectly recreate early internet culture. Even if you didn’t grow up with AIM, it still feels authentic.

However, the game is very short. A full playthrough is around an hour or less, and some players feel that the choices don’t change the ending as much as they expect.

But honestly, that’s kind of the point. Sometimes relationships just don’t work out, no matter what you say.

Pros

Unique storytelling through a chat interface

Very nostalgic early-2000s atmosphere

Realistic and relatable conversations

Completely free on Steam

Cons

Very short experience

Choices sometimes feel limited

Not much gameplay beyond reading and choosing dialogue

Final verdict:
A small indie game that tells a surprisingly emotional story. It’s short, but it sticks with you after you finish it.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that dialogue choices and branching paths do not significantly alter the final outcome of the story.

citations.review_text:
A short and sweet game with the sense of nostalgia when you were chatting with your friends back in 2000s on MSN Messenger during Windows XP days.

This game has multiple choices and Emily responds to them differently but ultimately never leads to a majorly different route.

There are also some easter eggs references to other games or celebrities or songs, pretty much this game is worth playing given it's free and it's only as much as 1 hour or less of playtime.

[i]Emily is Away[/i] is a short visual novel about maintaining relationships and drifting apart as you grow up. While the game was pretty cool, it didn’t really leave any impression on me.

Before I talk about the plot, I would like to say something about the game mechanics. What I found really cool and unique, was that after choosing a dialogue option you have to type it… Kind of. You just have to press any button on your keyboard to reveal a single letter. Which quickly became exhausting, especially if you wanted to replay the game to see if you could get a different ending. Turned out it was pointless, as no matter the choices made, the outcome was still the same- which was rather disappointing.

(Further review might contain spoilers.)

My negative review doesn’t mean the game was terrible… Or even bad. I think it just wasn’t that memorable, to not call it a waste of time. The dialogues with Emily are well-written, they feel really natural and not awkward at all (or they feel awkward when they have to be). But once again, it is such a shame that there aren’t more endings! The relationship with Emily was supposed to drift apart from the very beginning, so I understand that there wasn’t supposed to be any “happy” ending, but maybe adding something more than slight changes in some responses would be great. All the “Emily will remember this” notifications were pointless, as they didn’t really impact the story that much/at all.

What was really nice is not only the dialogues are done well, but Emily feels like a real person you would text on the internet or someone you might even know. She truly is a sweetheart at the very beginning, but as time passes, she’s clearly not doing well. Her admitting that her boyfriend isn’t always that great to her and avoiding the topic, when the player says they should break up, breaking up with him, then getting back together… Just like most people, she wants the best for everyone around her, which isn’t that good for her in …

Every review I read focuses on how nostalgic the game is, its "deep meaning" or how it reflects on relationships, drifting apart, and missed opportunities. I'm just a little frustrated because of the ending.
[spoiler]No matter how many times I played, I got the same ending. There's no positive scenario (at least I couldn't reach one and I tried 3 or 4 different paths), and that sucks. Emily will always want what didn't happen, and you'll both live with regret and drift apart, lol.[/spoiler]

I'm recommending it anyway because the John Cena icon achievement made me crack up, the nostalgia [i]is[/i] real and the game is free and fast anyway. Maybe you get more out of it.

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight the early 2000s internet aesthetics, including instant messaging layouts and computer sounds.

citations.review_text:
This game is nostalgia bait for millennials - a true call back to the aesthetics, some lingo, and experiences with relationships/friendships early on. Either one or both parties were typically immature, couldn't communicate or think properly, so things tended not to go well.

Hop on AIM/MSN messenger for one last ride, sweep your hair out of your eyes, and go forth. 

Also coldplay and snow patrol do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ suck.

So... this game has some funny nostalgic meme and game references if you enter specific usernames when starting the game, and I am glad that the devs decided to put some light-hearted content into the game, because the storyline of the game actually hit me in the feels a little bit. The last chapter was actually a little bit hard to get through, there were choices that I [i]didn't want to choose[/i] because I had a good idea of what the outcome would be. It was a bit on the brutal side.

I don't really know what to say about this game, but what I can say is: I'm glad that I played it, and if you have a bit of free time and want an easy +1 perfect game for your profile, check this one out. If you're a softie (not like me), bring tissues (which I didn't need).

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the typing mechanic as pressing any keyboard button to populate pre-written text letter by letter, which some found tedious during replays.

citations.review_text: I think the story is not engaging enough to keep playing. Maybe there's pretty good answer by the end of the story but I complete the game twice and both end is practically the same thing. Difference is emily date different dude. Also the typing mechanism get boring quick and tacky making the game longer that it need to. Like it work for some  moment but for the rest it felt like inconvenient

Great story. Just keep in mind that "branching narrative" is a misleading. Some decisions, light and major, happen off-screen that you have no control over and can make your character look like a massive jerk.

The decision of having to type the replies (see in the trailer how the messages are written? You have to type each letter/character to have it match the final message your character sends) is also a annoying. Just selecting the option and having it write for you would have been way better.

Steam doesn't have a mixed rating, so I will give it a recommend just because the game is free. If you had to pay, it would be a no. 

Light Spoiler: Spend an hour at it and don't bother with alternate paths. The endings are pretty much the same and reading the alternatives is better than redoing the game due to the typing issue.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game is very short, taking around one to two hours to complete.

citations.review_text:
Since I am playing the rest of the series, I had to drop a review for where it all started. It’s a nice, short hit of pure nostalgia that keeps you hooked for an hour or two. The retro messenger interface, the profile pictures, and the sound effects are perfect if you grew up in the early 2000s internet era. The story is simple but very engaging.

Although after you finish the story once, you might lose the motivation to play again just to see minor dialogue changes. Still, it is completely free and 100% worth your time. A perfect setup before jumping into Emily is Away Too.

[h3] 100% Achievement Review: Based on my experience completing all the (available) achievements. [/h3]

Feel free to follow my [u][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45897386/]Steam Curator[/url][/u] & [u][url=https://www.youtube.com/@Awijii]Youtube Channel[/url][/u] for more 100% reviews, videos & achievement content!

[h3]Title: Emily Is Away[/h3]

Summary: Interactive story game

Personal notes: A very short game based on the internet back in the early 2000's. Has a very cool style and aesthetic which depicts the time it was aiming to replicate. The story is decent, well paced and spans the course of multiple years which is cool. This being said, you have very little influence over this story in the grand scheme of things which is kind of frustrating. The achievements are super easy, all being story related or "hidden" icon related. Overall this game is decent considering it is free, I would recommend giving it a go if you want a quick story or to reminisce on the style from the old days of the internet. 

Time it took to complete: 2hrs

Most difficult achievement(s):
- Stanley didn't unlock this (Use the Stanley Parable Icon) 
- Write Some Fiction (Use the Elegy for a Dead World Icon)
- Vid Spilum Endalaust (Use the Sigur Ros Icon)

Difficulty rating: 
★★☆☆☆☆☆☆☆☆ 2/10

Overall rating: 
★★★★★☆☆☆☆☆ 5/10

citations.review_text:
Since I am playing the rest of the series, I had to drop a review for where it all started. It’s a nice, short hit of pure nostalgia that keeps you hooked for an hour or two. The retro messenger interface, the profile pictures, and the sound effects are perfect if you grew up in the early 2000s internet era. The story is simple but very engaging.

Although after you finish the story once, you might lose the motivation to play again just to see minor dialogue changes. Still, it is completely free and 100% worth your time. A perfect setup before jumping into Emily is Away Too.

Emily is Away is an interactive narrative experience developed and published by Kyle Seeley that proves a powerful story does not require elaborate graphics, complex gameplay systems, or lengthy cutscenes. Built around the familiar interface of an early-2000s instant messaging program, the game tells a deeply personal story about friendship, romance, growing apart, and the emotional uncertainty that accompanies the transition from adolescence into adulthood. What begins as a simple nostalgia trip gradually becomes an unexpectedly moving exploration of relationships and the choices that shape them.

The game's concept is remarkably simple. Players create a screen name, customize a profile, and communicate with friends through a chat client inspired by the internet culture of the early 2000s. The story unfolds across several years, with each chapter representing a different stage in the lives of the characters. Through these conversations, players build a relationship with Emily, a close friend whose connection with the protagonist evolves over time. The entire narrative is delivered through text messages, yet it manages to achieve a level of emotional impact that many larger and more ambitious games struggle to reach.

One of the most impressive aspects of Emily is Away is how authentically it recreates a specific era of online communication. The interface, profile customization, buddy lists, away messages, and music preferences all capture the atmosphere of a time before modern social media transformed the internet. For players who experienced instant messaging platforms firsthand, the game evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. For those unfamiliar with the period, it provides an intriguing glimpse into how digital relationships once developed through slower, more personal interactions.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that player choices do not significantly alter the narrative or prevent the characters from ultimately drifting apart.

citations.review_text:
Beware before you read - there will be spoilers about the outcome of the game. If you want to be surprised or keep things fresh, it's best to avoid reading this review.



This game is very short, very simple, but enjoyable. It hits really close to home and will make your heart ache in a way that feels a little all too real and familiar. I have gone out of my way to get all the steam achievements (basically, play the game your way, and do some easter eggs) and get all 3 main endings (the "goodbye", "bitter", and "excuse" endings). With that said, it doesn't matter what variation of the "goodbye" ending you get or the other endings you get, this game ends simply in one way - you and Emily drifting apart from one another. It's a feeling a lot of us 20+ individuals know all too well. You finish high school, maybe go to college, and your circle(s) from your time in high school inevitably grow apart (obviously, there is the rare exceptions). No matter what you may or may not have done, the relationship would've ended, and you would've grown apart. Sometimes, the best thing, is to let go, and keep moving forward in life. Not worry about the what-ifs or what could've been done to keep things in tact; only acceptance. That's exactly what this game displays and it does it in a very emotional way, but in a way that makes you feel less alone, and less sh**y about it. It's a natural part of being a living being. Heartbreaking, but warming at the same time. It's free and definitely worth the try (even if you don't end up liking it). 7/10 just for the lackluster choice of options and short run time (as displayed by my playtime in the review), but there are 2 follow-up's, if you want more. I'm about to play the second (Emily is Away Too) and I'm excited to see the improvements made! :3

Very short game, took me only 2.5 hours to casually 100%. First time I saw the game, it felt very incredible. However, after playing a few times and realizing choices don't matter, the story falls flat. There's definitely room for improvement in the story, and I'm assuming the second game has made these improvements. The game is free now, so there is no harm in playing through the game at least once, and I would recommend anyone into interactive narrative games to look into this series. Overall an average game, 6/10.
